questions.q: Define "imagery" in the context of literary analysis and list the five types of sensory imagery.
questions.a: Imagery is the use of language that appeals to the five senses to create a sensory experience for the reader. The five types are visual (sight), auditory (sound), tactile (touch), olfactory (smell), and gustatory (taste). A wrong answer that only mentions “descriptive words” or “pictures in the mind” reveals the student confuses imagery with general description and does not know the sensory classification required for board answers.

questions.q: In the chapter, the author writes: “The sun hammered the dunes, turning each grain into a tiny mirror.” Explain in your own words what sensory experience this sentence creates and which type of imagery dominates.
questions.a: The sentence creates a blinding, intense visual experience of sunlight reflecting off sand grains, dominated by visual imagery. The verb “hammered” adds a tactile sense of force, but the primary appeal is sight. A wrong answer that says “it shows the sun is hot” misses the sensory specificity and the identification of the dominant imagery type, indicating the student cannot separate the literal meaning from the sensory effect.

questions.q: Given the following new sentence about the same setting: “A dry wind scraped the skin, carrying the faint scent of camel dung and roasted cumin,” identify all the types of imagery present and underline the words that signal each type.
questions.a: Tactile: “scraped the skin”, “dry wind”. Olfactory: “scent of camel dung”, “roasted cumin”. Gustatory: “roasted cumin” (evokes taste). Visual: none explicitly. Auditory: none. A wrong answer that lists only “smell and touch” or misses “gustatory” shows the student cannot detect overlapping sensory cues in a single phrase, a skill needed for close reading in exams.

questions.q: Compare the imagery used to describe the desert at noon in the chapter with the imagery used for the early morning. How does the shift in sensory details reflect a change in mood or theme?
questions.a: At noon the imagery is harsh, blinding, oppressive (visual glare, tactile heat, silence), reinforcing the theme of extreme challenge. In the morning the imagery is cooler, softer, with auditory cues like bird calls and tactile relief, suggesting hope and the possibility of movement. A wrong answer that merely lists different images without linking the shift to mood or theme shows the student treats imagery as isolated decoration rather than a thematic tool.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the author’s choice to use predominantly tactile and visual imagery (rather than auditory or olfactory) in the passage describing Khetaram’s walk across the dunes. Justify your judgment with reference to the character’s experience.
questions.a: The choice is highly effective because Khetaram’s experience is physically gruelling; tactile imagery (burning soles, abrasive sand) makes the reader feel his bodily strain, while visual imagery (endless dunes, mirage) conveys the psychological vastness he must conquer. Auditory or olfactory details would distract from the solitary, body-centred struggle. A wrong answer that says “it is good because it describes well” without tying the sensory selection to character experience reveals an inability to evaluate authorial craft.

questions.q: Write a four-line descriptive paragraph about a dust storm in the Thar that uses at least three different types of imagery and deliberately avoids visual imagery.
questions.a: A strong response might be: “The wind howled like a wounded animal (auditory), grit stung my cheeks and coated my tongue with alkali (tactile, gustatory), and the air grew thick with the musk of wet sand after rain (olfactory).” A poor response that includes visual words (“brown cloud”, “dark sky”) or uses only one sense shows the student cannot consciously control sensory selection, a skill needed for creative writing tasks in the board.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ language refers to the deliberate use of vivid adjectives, strong verbs, sensory details, and figurative expressions to create a concrete mental picture of a person, place, object, or experience.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ a scorching afternoon in the Thar Desert to a friend who has never left a hill station.
What is Descriptive language? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Descriptive language refers to the deliberate use of vivid adjectives, strong verbs, sensory details, and figurative expressions to create a concrete mental picture of a person, place, object, or experience.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Descriptive language?
questions.a: Students often believe that “imagery” means only visual description (pictures in the mind) and that any adjective counts as imagery.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently extract a descriptive passage from the chapter, label each sensory image with its type, explain the combined effect on the reader’s perception of the Thar Desert, and write a structured PEEL paragraph linking that effect to the theme of duty or connectivity.
